1.summary: James tells believers to count trials as joy because testing produces endurance, to ask God for wisdom without doubting, to recognize that temptation comes from our own desires while every good gift comes from God, and to be doers of the word, not hearers only.
1.lookfor: Notice the mirror image, and James's definition of pure religion at the end.

names.name: James
names.gloss: The Lord's brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

insights.title: A servant, not a brother
insights.body: James introduces himself only as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (1:1), not as Jesus' brother. He once thought Jesus had lost his mind.

insights.title: The twelve tribes scattered
insights.body: He writes to the twelve tribes in the dispersion (1:1), Jewish believers living outside the land, perhaps scattered by persecution after Stephen's death.

insights.title: Joy in trials
insights.body: Count it all joy when you fall into trials, because testing your faith produces endurance, and endurance makes you complete (1:2-4). Joy comes from what the trial produces, not the trial itself.

insights.title: Ask for wisdom
insights.body: If anyone lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach (1:5). God doesn't scold us for asking.

insights.title: The Father of lights
insights.body: Every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning (1:17). He made the sun and stars, which shift and change; he doesn't.

insights.title: Doers of the word
insights.body: Be doers of the word, not hearers only (1:22). Hearing without doing is like glancing in a mirror and forgetting your face (1:23-24). Echoes Jesus' parable of the two builders.

insights.title: Pure religion
insights.body: Pure religion before God is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction and to keep oneself unstained by the world (1:27). Care for the vulnerable and personal holiness together.

insights.title: Quick to listen
insights.body: Be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger (1:19). Which of the three is hardest for you?

2.summary: James condemns favoritism toward the rich in church gatherings, since God chose the poor to be rich in faith and the royal law commands love of neighbor; he then argues that faith without works is dead, citing Abraham and Rahab.
2.lookfor: Notice the vivid scene of two visitors at a meeting, and how James uses Abraham differently from Paul.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: Who showed his faith by offering Isaac.

names.name: Isaac
names.gloss: Abraham's son, offered on the altar.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: The prostitute of Jericho who hid the spies.

insights.title: The gold ring
insights.body: A man with gold rings and fine clothes is given a good seat; a poor man in shabby clothes is told to stand or sit on the floor (2:2-3). Gold rings marked the Roman equestrian class, the wealthy elite.

insights.title: God chose the poor
insights.body: Didn't God choose those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom? (2:5). And it's the rich who oppress you and drag you into court (2:6).

insights.title: The royal law
insights.body: The royal law, according to Scripture, is love your neighbor as yourself (2:8). Royal because it is the King's law, and Jesus called it the second great command.

insights.title: Mercy triumphs
insights.body: Judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy; mercy triumphs over judgment (2:13).

insights.title: Dead faith
insights.body: Faith without works is dead (2:17, 2:26). If someone lacks food and you say go in peace, be warmed and filled, without giving them anything, what good is it? (2:15-16).

insights.title: James and Paul
insights.body: James says a person is justified by works and not by faith only (2:24); Paul says by faith apart from works of the law. They use words differently: Paul attacks works as a way to earn God's favor; James attacks faith that is only talk. Both agree real faith produces action.

insights.title: Even the demons believe
insights.body: You believe God is one; you do well. The demons also believe, and shudder (2:19). Agreeing with the Shema isn't saving faith.

insights.title: Faith in action
insights.body: James asks what good faith is if it doesn't help someone in need. Who needs your faith to take practical form this week?

3.summary: James warns that teachers will be judged more strictly and that the tongue, though small, is like a bit, a rudder and a spark that sets a forest ablaze; no one can tame it, yet blessing and cursing shouldn't come from one mouth; he contrasts earthly wisdom marked by envy with the peaceable wisdom from above.
3.lookfor: Notice the series of images for the tongue, and the list of qualities of wisdom from above.

insights.title: Not many teachers
insights.body: Not many of you should become teachers, for we'll receive stricter judgment (3:1). Teachers shape others with their words, so their words weigh more.

insights.title: Bit, rudder and spark
insights.body: A small bit turns a horse, a small rudder steers a great ship, a small fire sets a forest ablaze (3:3-5). Everyday images from riding, sailing and dry hillsides.

insights.title: The course of nature
insights.body: The tongue sets on fire the course of life and is itself set on fire by Gehenna (3:6). Gehenna was the valley outside Jerusalem associated with burning and judgment; this is its only use outside the Gospels.

insights.title: Blessing and cursing
insights.body: With the tongue we bless God and curse people made in his likeness (3:9). To curse a person is to insult their Maker.

insights.title: Springs and fig trees
insights.body: Can a spring pour out fresh and bitter water? Can a fig tree produce olives? (3:11-12). Jesus said a tree is known by its fruit.

insights.title: Wisdom from above
insights.body: The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere (3:17). Real wisdom is known by its character, not its cleverness.

insights.title: Your words
insights.body: James says words can bless or burn. Whom have your words hurt recently, and whom could they build up today?

4.summary: James traces quarrels to selfish desires, calls double-minded friendship with the world adultery against God, promises that God gives grace to the humble and draws near to those who draw near to him, warns against judging others and against boasting about tomorrow's plans.
4.lookfor: Notice the series of commands in verses 7 to 10, and the mist image near the end.

insights.title: Where fights come from
insights.body: What causes quarrels among you? Isn't it your passions at war within you? (4:1). External conflict grows from internal desire. You don't have because you don't ask, or ask with wrong motives (4:2-3).

insights.title: Adulterers
insights.body: You adulterers! Friendship with the world is hostility toward God (4:4). The prophets called Israel's idolatry adultery against God, her husband.

insights.title: Grace to the humble
insights.body: God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (4:6), from Proverbs. Peter quotes the same verse.

insights.title: Draw near
insights.body: Submit to God; resist the devil and he will flee; draw near to God and he will draw near to you (4:7-8). Ten commands in quick succession, a call to repentance.

insights.title: Double-minded
insights.body: Purify your hearts, you double-minded (4:8). The word dipsychos, two-souled, appears only in James: divided loyalty between God and the world.

insights.title: Merchants' plans
insights.body: Today or tomorrow we'll go to such a city, spend a year, trade and make a profit (4:13). Travelling merchants were common; James doesn't condemn planning, but planning without God.

insights.title: A mist
insights.body: What is your life? A mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes (4:14). So say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (4:15).

insights.title: If the Lord wills
insights.body: James calls us to hold plans loosely. What plan of yours do you need to hand over to God?

5.summary: James denounces rich oppressors who hoarded wealth and withheld workers' wages, urges believers to be patient like a farmer until the Lord comes, not to grumble or swear oaths, and to pray in every circumstance, with elders anointing the sick, confessing sins to one another, and turning back those who wander.
5.lookfor: Notice the examples of patience and prayer from Job and Elijah.

names.name: Job
names.gloss: The man who endured great suffering and saw God's purpose.

names.name: Elijah
names.gloss: The prophet whose prayer stopped and started the rain.

insights.title: Withheld wages
insights.body: The wages of the workers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, cry out (5:4). Day laborers lived hand to mouth; the law required wages to be paid the same day.

insights.title: Early and late rain
insights.body: The farmer waits patiently for the early and late rains (5:7). In Israel, autumn rains softened the ground for planting and spring rains filled out the grain.

insights.title: Job's endurance
insights.body: You have heard of Job's endurance and seen the end the Lord brought about: the Lord is full of compassion and mercy (5:11).

insights.title: Let your yes be yes
insights.body: Don't swear, by heaven or earth; let your yes be yes and your no be no (5:12), almost word for word from Jesus.

insights.title: Anointing the sick
insights.body: Is anyone sick? Call the elders to pray and anoint with oil in the Lord's name (5:14). Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God; the disciples anointed the sick on their mission.

insights.title: Elijah was like us
insights.body: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, yet he prayed and it didn't rain for three and a half years (5:17). The prayer of a righteous person is powerful (5:16).

insights.title: Confess to one another
insights.body: Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so you may be healed (5:16). Healing here may be bodily and relational at once.

insights.title: Bring someone back
insights.body: James ends: whoever turns a sinner back from wandering saves a soul (5:20). Is there someone drifting whom you could gently reach out to?

intro.who: James (1:1), traditionally the brother of Jesus who led the Jerusalem church, a man who didn't believe in Jesus during his ministry but saw him risen. Some scholars think it was written later in his name.
intro.when: If by James, between about AD 45 and his death in AD 62, possibly one of the earliest New Testament writings.
intro.why: Written to Jewish believers scattered abroad (1:1), it reads like Old Testament wisdom literature and echoes Jesus' Sermon on the Mount. Its aim is practical: faith that is real shows itself in endurance, doing the word, care for the poor, controlled speech, humility and prayer.

outline.title: Trials, wisdom and doing the word
Taming the tongue; wisdom from above
